Navajo is an Athabaskan language spoken by the Navajo people across the southwestern United States, most notably in the Navajo Nation spanning Arizona, New Mexico, and Utah. It is the most widely spoken Native American language north of Mexico and exemplifies polysynthetic and highly agglutinative verbal morphology. The language is part of the Athabaskan family, linguistically related to Apache, Dene, also called Chipewyan, and various Pacific Northwest languages, all part of the larger Dene-Yeniseian hypothesis that links Siberian and North American languages together. Navajo features an unusually complex verb system with extensive aspectual distinctions and directional prefixes, making it a highly synthetic language where verbs encode extensive information about aspect, mode, and directionality through both prefixes and stem changes. The language has roughly 150,000 to 170,000 native speakers, primarily on the Navajo Nation, though it is endangered due to declining youth fluency despite official status and school programs dedicated to its preservation. One of the few Native American languages with a substantial and stable speaker base, Navajo gained significant fame during World War II when Code Talkers used the language's complexity and low number of non-native speakers to transmit encrypted military messages, making it central to the history of military cryptography in the twentieth century. The language has a unique writing system and considerable written literature, with recent revival efforts focusing on digital resources, schools, and community initiatives to reverse language shift. Unlike neighboring Pueblo languages, Navajo uses nominative-accusative alignment, similar to most Indo-European languages.
